rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham is an exemplary community whose worldly and afterlife benefits make him a model for anyone able to benefit; believers should follow him in monotheism and obedience rather than merely imitate ancestors.
rows.anchor: أي أباكم الأعظم إمام الموحدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qānit means sincerely devoted to God, the sovereign whose command governs everything without self-interest; ḥanīf means one who inclines with divine commands and prohibitions, abrogated or not.
rows.anchor: قانتا } أي مخلصا { لله } أي الملك الذي له الأمر كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dropped nūn in يكن is concise, emphatic negation that prevents misreading before the sentence is complete and denies Abraham even the least associationism; polytheism follows caprice.
rows.anchor: حذف نون { يكن } منها إيجازا وتقريبا للفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural of paucity in His favors signals that every blessing Abraham thanked for was little beside God's generosity; whoever thanks for little will all the more thank for much, and God will increase him.
rows.anchor: مشيرا إلى ذلك بجمع القلة وإلى أن الشاكر على القليل يشكر إذا أتاه الكثير من باب الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The audience should thank God in imitation of Abraham so that God may increase them; God chose Abraham completely and guided him through the greatest clarification and fullest enabling to the straight, tolerant monotheistic path.
rows.anchor: اجتباه } أي اختاره اختيارا تاما { وهداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham upheld justice and the straight path, unlike the mute figure in the preceding parable.
rows.anchor: فكان ممن يأمر بالعدل وهو على صراط مستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham received worldly good as an enduring good name and praise, alongside prophetic, righteous, royal, and numerous descendants.
rows.anchor: ورزقه في أولاده من النبوة والصلاح والملك والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah aims to assure the Prophet of respite, forbearance, and gentle treatment toward those he calls until they become the largest community, honoring him; its opening letters allude to this for the perceptive.
rows.anchor: مقصودها الإعلام بإمهال المدعوين والحلم عنهم والترفق بهم إلى أن يكونوا أكثر الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā's articulation at the tongue tip and upper incisors symbolizes force, elevation, broad propagation, and many followers; its phonetic qualities signal a private mission becoming public and jolting all nations.
rows.anchor: إشارة بمخرجها الذي هو من رأس اللسان وأصول الثنيتين العليين إلى قوة أمر وانتشاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hā's deep-throat articulation and whispered, lax, open, low, hidden qualities signal weakness, concealment, and severe hardship.
rows.anchor: الهاء بمخرجها من أقصى الحلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hā's imāla reading signals weakness, while the more common tafkhīm reading signals high rank and strength.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الإمالة للهاء تشير إلى شدة الضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Ṭā-Hā means O man, it signals the Prophet's strength, high standing, fame, and growing followers; if it evokes treading earth, it signals firm power and dominion.
rows.anchor: معنى الحرفين : يا رجل

rows.speaker: ابن الفرات
rows.claim: Ibn al-Furāt dates the Abyssinian migration to the eighth year of the Prophet's mission.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن الفرات في تأريخه أن هحر الحبشة كانت قي السنة الثامنة من المبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that chronology and the account of Umar's conversion, the author infers that this surah or its opening was revealed near the Abyssinian migration.
rows.anchor: نزول هذه السورة أو أولها كان قرب هجرة الحبشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Numerical allusions predict the disbelievers' weakening at Badr al-Mawʿid in revelation year nine, the first victory at Hudaybiyya in year eleven, and the Hijra as the beginning of victory in year five.
rows.anchor: في السنة التاسعة من نزولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further counts predict actual victory at the Great Battle of Badr in revelation year seven; counting the two letters predicts Mecca's conquest in year thirteen and Ṭāʾif's completion in year fourteen, while their names predict Islam's spread under Umar in year eighteen.
rows.anchor: وبعدد حرفي اسمها لا بعدد اسميها إلى أنه في السنة الثالثة عشر من نزولها يكون بفتح الأكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala names God as supremely powerful and forbearing, the supreme King, the source of universal mercy, and the one who completes blessing for those guided by His favor.
rows.anchor: بسم } الواسع الحلم التام القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā-Hā signifies complete release from fear and a great, wholesome renown spreading across every region, from the One who encompasses the unseen and to whom all affairs return.
rows.anchor: أي تخلص بالغ من كل ما يخشى

rows.speaker: هشام
rows.claim: Hishām, citing Ibn Isḥāq, says this surah and the one before it are among the earliest Meccan revelations.
rows.anchor: قال هشام في تهذيب السيرة

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the emigrants found safety and freedom to worship under the Negus, while Quraysh sent gifts and sought their return; the Negus insisted on hearing the refugees first.
rows.anchor: عن أم سلمة بنت أم أمية بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: جعفر بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Jaʿfar explains that Islam called people emerging from idolatry and social abuses to worship one God and uphold truth, trust, kinship, good neighborliness, and avoid bloodshed and vice.
rows.anchor: جعفر بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm Salama's report continues: Muslims were commanded to worship God alone, pray, give alms, and fast; after believing, they were persecuted and sought refuge with the Negus, who heard Jaʿfar recite Maryam, wept with his bishops, recognized a shared source with Moses, and sent Quraysh's envoys away with their gifts.
rows.anchor: به شيئا , وأمرنا بالصلاة والزكاة والصيام

rows.speaker: أم عبد الله بنت أبي حثمة
rows.claim: Umm ʿAbd Allah bint Abi Hathma recalls that Umar, still a polytheist, showed unexpected tenderness when she said persecution had forced her and her husband to emigrate to Abyssinia.
rows.anchor: عن أمه أم عبدالله بنت أبي حثمة رضي الله عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the same account, ʿĀmir doubts Umar will ever accept Islam, joking that even al-Khaṭṭāb's donkey would convert first because Umar was so harsh.
rows.anchor: لايسيلم الذي رأيت حتى يسلم حمار الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says Umar's conversion began with his secretly Muslim sister Fāṭima, her husband Saʿīd, Nuʿaym, and Khabbāb, who taught them Qur'an; Umar set out armed toward Muhammad and a gathering of nearly forty Muslims.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق : وكان إسلام عمر فيما بلغني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umar says he intends to kill Muhammad for dividing Quraysh and denouncing its religion; Nuʿaym warns Quraysh would not let him go free afterward and redirects him to his converted sister and brother-in-law.
rows.anchor: أريد محمدا هذا الصابىء الذي فرق أمر قريش وسفه أحلامها وعاب دينها وسب آلهتها

rows.speaker: نعيم بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Nuʿaym tells Umar that his sister Fāṭima and brother-in-law Saʿīd have accepted Muhammad's faith, and sends him to confront them instead.
rows.anchor: فقال له نعيم رضي الله عنه : والله ! لقد غرتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Fāṭima and Saʿīd's home, Khabbāb is teaching them Ṭā-Hā; they hide the page, and Umar demands to know what he heard.
rows.anchor: خباب بن الأرت رضي الله عنه وعنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Umar insists he heard them following Muhammad, Fāṭima and Saʿīd confess their faith; seeing Fāṭima's blood, he regrets his violence, asks for the page, washes at her insistence, reads Ṭā-Hā, and praises it.
rows.anchor: قالت له أخته وختنه رضي الله عنهما : نعم ! قد أسلمنا

rows.speaker: خباب بن الأرت
rows.claim: Khabbāb hopes Umar is the one singled out by the Prophet's prayer, which he says he heard the previous day asking God to strengthen Islam through Abu al-Ḥakam or Umar.
rows.anchor: فلما سمع ذلك خباب رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: حمزة بن عبد المطلب
rows.claim: When the Muslims fear Umar's armed arrival, Hamza says to admit him: if he comes with good intent they can give it, and if with evil they can kill him with his own sword.
rows.anchor: فقال حمزة بن عبد المطلب رضي الله عنه : فأذن له

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet admits Umar and rebukes him, asking what brought him and warning that a calamity will come upon him if he does not stop.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ائذن له

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar tells the Prophet he came to believe in God, His Messenger, and what God sent; the Prophet's takbīr lets the household know Umar has become Muslim and strengthens the Muslims.
rows.anchor: قال عمر : يارسول الله ! جئتك لأومن بالله وبرسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account is attributed to Medinan transmitters; another cited chronology places Umar's conversion three days after Hamza's, citing Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn al-Jawzī.
rows.anchor: فهذا حديث الرواة من أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: نافع مولى عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Nafiʿ, freedman of ʿAbd Allah ibn Umar, transmits that Umar asked which Qurayshi spread news fastest, told Jamīl he had become Muslim, and was immediately publicly denounced as a convert.
rows.anchor: وحدثني نافع مولى عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar says he followed his father as Jamīl announced Umar's conversion; Umar confirmed it, fought Quraysh until exhausted, and said three hundred Muslims could have held their ground.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنهما : وغدوت أتبع أثره

rows.speaker: شيخ من قريش
rows.claim: An unnamed Qurayshi elder approaches the crowd, then intervenes on Umar's behalf, asking whether Banū ʿAdī would surrender him.
rows.anchor: إذ أقبل شيخ من قريش عليه حلة حبرة وقميص موشى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurayshi elder asks why the crowd is gathered, says Umar chose his own course, and asks whether Banū ʿAdī would surrender him; the crowd disperses as though stripped of a garment.
rows.anchor: رجل اختار لنفسه أمرا فماذا تريدون

rows.speaker: يونس عن ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī transmits through Yūnus from Ibn Isḥāq a poem attributed to Umar after conversion, praising God's favor and saying his sister's Qur'an recitation and prayer softened and guided him.
rows.anchor: أن يونس روى عن ابن إسحاق أن عمر قال حين أسلم رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah honors the Prophet by assuring him that gentle patience will draw hearts and grow his community; God calmed and protected early Muslims, softened Umar into a defender, and prevents their annihilation like the peoples of Noah and Hud.
rows.anchor: تشريف هذا النبي الكريم صلى الله عليه وسلم بإعلامه بالرفق بأمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Maryam ends with the destruction of earlier nations while Muhammad had few believers, this surah reassures him that his people will not be wiped out by punishment as those nations were.
rows.anchor: لما ختم تلك بإهلاك القرون وإبادة الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial that the Qur'an was sent to make the Prophet suffer addresses his fear that few would follow him after his people were destroyed; instead it is a reminder for those who fear God.
rows.anchor: أي بتعب قلبك بكونك من أقل المرسلين تابعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder points to people promised glad tidings at the preceding surah's close: the community will include enough pious believers to match the Qur'an's miraculous stature and endurance.
rows.anchor: ممن أشرنا في آخر التي قبلها إلى بشارته إيماء إلى أنه سيكون فيهم من المتقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an gathers laws, counsel, spiritual insights, knowledge, manners, histories, and interests of both worlds from earlier scriptures, and exceeds them; the community's size reflects its book's greatness.
rows.anchor: أي أعظم الكتب , الجامع لكل خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illā here means but; a poetic line illustrates an exception that functions as a qualification of praise.
rows.anchor: غير أن سيوفهم بهن فلول من قراع الكتائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun tanzīlan signals gradual revelation, giving people time, answering doubts, opening hearts, calming them, and extending blessings through angel visits; a messenger also removes their excuse that no warning came.
rows.anchor: إلى أنه يتمهل عليهم ترفقا بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from first-person plural to third-person the One who created evokes divine greatness; earth is named first to show mercy for its inhabitants as the surah seeks to fill it with faith.
rows.anchor: مقدما ما اقتضى الحال تقديمه من سكن المدعوين المعتنى بتذكرتهم وهداية من أريد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After earth, the text ascends to the heavens as the locus of revelation, from the House of Might to the guarded storehouse of the Throne; God created both in six days though able to create them instantly.
rows.anchor: أتبعها محل الإنزال على سبيل الترقي من بيت العزة إلى ما كنزه في خزانة العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān names the giver of universal blessings to obedient and disobedient alike; the verse establishes kingship, since power alone does not make one a king.
rows.anchor: الوصف المفيض للنعم العامة للطائع والعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā means God undertook governance of creation alone, using the familiar image of a king sitting upright on a throne; it entails neither an actual seat nor physical location.
rows.anchor: أي أخذ في تدبير ذلك منفردا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The hadith in Muslim that hearts are between two of God's fingers means God has immense, effortless power to turn hearts as He wills, not a literal finger.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو رضي الله عنهما ' القلوب بين إصبعين

rows.speaker: حجة الإسلام الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī is cited for taking the fingers in the hadith figuratively: the image conveys God's power over hearts, not a physical finger.
rows.anchor: نبه على ذلك حجة الإسلام الغزالي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī likewise treats so-and-so's open hand as a metaphor for generosity, even where there is no literal hand or extension.
rows.anchor: ومنه أخذ الزمخشري أن يد فلان مبسوطة كناية عن جواد وإن لم يكن هناك يد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything in the heavens, earth, between them, and beneath moist soil belongs to God, whether what lies below is nothingness or another created realm.
rows.anchor: وما تحت الثرى } وهو التراب الندي
